newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street claws back some lost ground by midday.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street claws back some lost ground by midday.

text.p: U.S. stocks recovered some lost territory on Tuesday, reassured Japan was not planning an imminent sale of its U.S. government bond holdings, but the market's bounce was hampered by some lurking inflation fears.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average, which sank Monday after comments by Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto sparked fears his country might sell U.S. Treasuries, was up about 46 points at 7651, below its session high of 7686.
A buying spree by bargain hunters drove the Dow higher and caused the New York Stock Exchange to set trading curbs.

Hashimoto, responding to a question at Columbia University, was quoted as saying Japan in the past had been tempted to sell U.S. government bond holdings and boost its gold reserves but had not done so. Later a senior Ministry of Finance official said U.S. government bonds were an essential investment tool within Japan's foreign reserves.
"The tempest in the Japanese teapot has calmed down," said Alfred Kugel, Stein Roe senior investment strategist. He said Hashimoto's comments had provided an excuse to take profits.
Analysts said the Dow's rebound Tuesday lost some steam after the release of stronger-than-forecast consumer confidence data.
The Conference Board, a private business research group, said its index of U.S. consumer confidence rose to 129.6 for the month, its highest since August 1969.
Ken Goldstein, senior economist at the Conference Board, told Reuters Financial Television, that U.S. prices were not completely in check, adding he expected an uptick in inflation down the road.
The long bond was up 4/32, with its yield dipping to 6.70 percent yield.
Traders said the market remained jittery after Monday's declines.
"Yesterday's sell-off was significant," Warren Epstein, director of trading at Richard Rosenblatt, said. "People are just more cautious."

Among individual issues, shares of PacifiCare Health Systems Inc fell sharply after the company said its second-quarter earnings would fall short of analysts' estimates. Its stock was down 17-1/2 at 36-1/2.

Bristol-Myers Squibb Co was up 5-1/4 points at 81-5/8 in brisk trade. A U.S. Food and Drug Administration advisory panel voted unanimously to approve the company's paclitaxel drug as a second-line therapy for Kaposi's sarcoma, a cancer affecting 20,000 AIDS patients.
Shares of International Business Machines Corp, a Dow component, were up 2-1/2 at 90-1/2. Investment firm Morgan Stanley said it raised its price target on IBM to $105 per share from $93.
